title: Inflation: why cash slowly loses value

sections.body: Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. When prices rise, each dollar buys a little less. Money sitting in cash keeps the same number on the screen but quietly loses buying power.
Example: at 3% inflation, $10,000 kept in cash for 20 years will only buy what about $5,540 buys today.
Rule of 72 works here too: 72 ÷ 3 = 24, so at 3% inflation prices roughly double, and cash buys about half as much, in around 24 years.

items: Cash is still right for short-term needs and your emergency fund.
For long-term goals, money usually needs to grow faster than inflation to keep its value.
Compare savings rates to inflation. A 1% account during 3% inflation loses buying power.

sections.label: See what inflation does to your cash

quiz.q: What does inflation do to money held as cash?
quiz.why: The balance stays the same but prices go up, so it buys less.

quiz.q: At about 3% inflation, roughly how long until prices double?
Your savings account pays 1% and inflation is 3%. What happens to your buying power?
options: It shrinks by about 2% a year
quiz.why: Your money grows 1% but prices grow 3%, so you fall behind by about 2% a year.
